title: Newar food: a guide to the valley's own cuisine
meta_description: A guide to Newar food in the Kathmandu Valley: samay baji, bara, chatamari, choila, yomari and juju dhau, the feasts behind them and where to eat them.
summary: Newar food is the traditional cuisine of the Kathmandu Valley's oldest people. It is built on baji (beaten rice), buffalo, black soybeans, mustard oil, ginger and garlic, and tied to a calendar of festivals. Start with samay baji, bara, chatamari and choila, finish with juju dhau, and eat in Kirtipur, Patan and Bhaktapur rather than Thamel.

sections.heading: Why Newar food is its own cuisine
paras: The Newars built the cities of the Kathmandu Valley, and for centuries they were its merchants, farmers, priests and craftspeople. Their language, Nepal Bhasa, their festivals and their kitchens developed apart from the rest of Nepal, inside a fertile valley with rice paddies, buffalo and busy trade routes to Tibet and India.

The result is a cuisine that most visitors never meet, because tourist menus in Thamel lean towards momo, dal bhat and pizza. Newar food is sharper and more varied. It uses beaten rice instead of boiled rice at feasts, buffalo meat in many forms, black soybeans, fermented and pickled vegetables, mustard oil, ginger, garlic and timur, the tingling Himalayan pepper related to Sichuan pepper. Almost every dish has a place in the ritual year: a festival it belongs to, a god it is offered to first, or a stage of life it marks.
If you eat only one thing, make it a samay baji plate. If you eat for a day, follow the plan below.

sections.heading: Samay baji, the plate offered to the gods
paras: Samay baji is the Newar ritual plate, offered to deities at festivals and family rituals and then shared among the people present. It is also the best introduction to the cuisine. A typical plate holds a mound of baji, the flattened, dry beaten rice that is the base of every Newar feast; choila, buffalo meat grilled and tossed with chilli, garlic, ginger and mustard oil; black soybeans fried with spices; a boiled or fried egg; slivers of raw ginger and garlic; a potato pickle; and often a bara and a small cup of aila, the Newar rice spirit.

Each part has meaning, and families argue about the correct list. You will find samay baji on the menu of almost every Newar eatery in Kirtipur, Patan and Bhaktapur, served on a leaf plate or a brass tray.

sections.heading: Dishes to know before you order
paras: Newar menus can look unfamiliar. These are the dishes we would order for a first-time visitor, roughly from mild to adventurous.
list: Bara, also called wo: a thick patty of ground black lentils fried on a flat iron pan, plain or topped with egg or minced meat.
Chatamari: a thin rice-flour bread cooked on a griddle and topped with egg, minced meat or vegetables, often called Newar pizza.
Choila: buffalo meat, grilled or roasted, then mixed with mustard oil, chilli, garlic and ginger; haku choila is the darker version grilled over a straw fire.
Aloo tama: a sour soup of potato and fermented bamboo shoot, eaten across the valley.
Kwati: a soup of nine kinds of sprouted beans, eaten on the full moon of Janai Purnima in August.
Yomari: a steamed rice-flour dumpling shaped like a fig, filled with chaku (molasses) and sesame, or with khuwa, made for Yomari Punhi in December.
Kachila: finely minced raw buffalo meat marinated with spices and mustard oil, a centrepiece of feasts.
Sapu mhicha and swanpuka: buffalo leaf tripe stuffed with bone marrow, and lungs filled with a spiced batter, both fried. For the adventurous.
Takha: buffalo meat set in its own jelly, a winter dish.
Juju dhau: thick, sweet buffalo-milk curd set in clay bowls, the pride of Bhaktapur. The name means king of curds.
Aila and thwon: aila is a clear distilled spirit made from rice or millet; thwon is a milky, mildly alcoholic rice beer.

sections.heading: Food and the festival calendar
paras: Many Newar dishes appear on the table because of the date. Festivals follow the lunar calendar and move each year by a few weeks, so check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: A day of Newar eating
paras: If you want to taste the range in a single day, this is the route we give friends visiting from abroad. It needs a car or taxi for the hops and a good appetite.
list: Breakfast in Kathmandu's old town: hot bara from a griddle near Asan, with sweet milk tea.
Mid-morning in Patan: chatamari with egg in a small eatery near Durbar Square, then a walk through the metalworkers' lanes to make room.
Lunch in Kirtipur: a full samay baji plate on a terrace looking back over the valley, with a small cup of aila if you like.
Afternoon in Bhaktapur: a clay bowl of juju dhau on the steps of Nyatapola, and a look at the potters' square.
Evening: a long Newar or Nepali set dinner in a restored house, or a home meal arranged by your guide, where you will meet kachila, aloo tama and pickles you have not seen yet.

sections.heading: Where to eat Newar food
paras: Kirtipur, on its ridge south-west of Kathmandu, has a cluster of Newar restaurants near the old town where families come on Saturdays for samay baji with a view. In Patan, small eateries in the lanes around Durbar Square serve bara, chatamari and choila; Honacha, just off the square, has been feeding locals for generations from a dark, low room. Bhaktapur is the place for juju dhau, sold by the bowl around Taumadhi and Dattatreya squares, and for small kitchens serving wo and samay baji to people who live there.

In Kathmandu itself, look in the old town between Asan, Indra Chowk and Kathmandu Durbar Square, where tiny shops fry bara at breakfast. Several heritage hotels and restaurants in restored houses serve long Newar or Nepali set dinners for visitors, a good choice for a first night. For the full experience, the best meal is in a home, which a local guide can arrange.

sections.heading: How to eat like a guest
paras: At a traditional Newar feast, called bhwe, guests sit in rows on mats on the floor, and men of the host family serve course after course on to leaf plates. The order of seating follows age and status, and the eldest are served first. Eat with your right hand. Accept a little of everything, as refusing outright can seem rude; it is fine to leave food on the plate.

Nepalis observe jutho, the idea that anything touched by your mouth or saliva becomes impure. Do not offer food from your plate, do not drink from a shared bottle by touching it to your lips, and do not put a used spoon back into a serving dish. When aila is poured from a height into your cup, you may touch it to your lips and set it down. Wash your hands before and after the meal, and wait for the host to begin.

sections.heading: Vegetarians and careful stomachs
paras: Newar food is meat-heavy at feasts, but much of it is vegetarian: bara, plain chatamari, aloo tama, kwati, yomari, pickles and juju dhau. Ask for vegetable choila made with mushrooms or soybeans, which many restaurants now serve. Vegans should know that ghee and curd appear often.

For a sensitive stomach, choose food cooked hot in front of you, skip raw kachila and salads, and drink bottled or filtered water. Go slowly with aila, and with juju dhau on your first day. Most Newar eateries we use are where our guides' own families eat.

faqs.q: What is the most famous Newar dish?
faqs.a: Samay baji is the best known Newar food, a ritual plate of beaten rice, spiced buffalo choila, black soybeans, egg, ginger, garlic and pickles, often with bara and aila. Bara and chatamari are the most popular snacks, and juju dhau, the sweet curd of Bhaktapur, is the most famous sweet. Yomari is the festival favourite in December.

faqs.q: Where can I eat authentic Newar food in Kathmandu?
faqs.a: The best places are in the old Newar towns: Kirtipur's cluster of Newar restaurants, the eateries around Patan Durbar Square such as Honacha, and small kitchens in Bhaktapur near Taumadhi and Dattatreya squares. In Kathmandu's old town, look around Asan and Indra Chowk. A home meal arranged by a local guide is even better.

Chatamari is a thin, round rice-flour bread cooked on a hot griddle and topped with egg, minced buffalo or chicken, or vegetables, then covered while it cooks. It is often called Newar pizza, though it is thinner and lighter. It is a common snack and festival food, and Newar eateries in Patan, Kirtipur and Bhaktapur cook it to order.

Juju dhau means king of curds in Nepal Bhasa, the Newar language. It is a rich, slightly sweet curd made from buffalo milk and set in unglazed clay bowls, which absorb moisture and help it thicken. Bhaktapur is famous for it. Eat it fresh, on the day it is bought, as it does not keep well or travel.

Some dishes are hot, especially choila, kachila and the chilli pickles, but many are mild, flavoured with ginger, garlic, cumin, turmeric, mustard oil and timur pepper. Spice levels vary between kitchens. Pickles are often served on the side, so you can add heat as you like. Ask for less chilli and most cooks will adjust.

Yes. Bara, plain chatamari, aloo tama, kwati bean soup, yomari, achar pickles, beaten rice and juju dhau are all vegetarian, and many restaurants now offer mushroom or soybean choila. At a feast, tell the host in advance, and they will usually prepare vegetarian versions. Strict vegans should ask about ghee and curd, which are common.

Aila is a clear, strong Newar spirit distilled at home from rice or millet, served at festivals, feasts and rituals and offered to deities. It is traditionally poured from a height out of a spouted vessel into small clay cups. It is often much stronger than it tastes, so sip slowly. Thwon, the milky rice beer, is gentler.

Yomari Punhi falls on the full moon of the Nepali month of Mangsir, usually in December, at the end of the rice harvest. Newar families make yomari dumplings filled with molasses and sesame or sweet milk solids, offer them to deities and to the stored grain, and eat them together. Dates move each year, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is a Newar feast called and what happens at it?
faqs.a: A Newar feast is called bhwe. Guests sit in rows on mats on the floor and are served many courses on leaf plates by men of the host family, starting with beaten rice and ending with curd and sweets. Seating follows age and status. Feasts mark weddings, rice-feeding ceremonies, festivals and guthi gatherings, the community associations of Newar life.
